alt: The bourgeoisie own the means of production and the proletariat must sell their labour, an unequal and exploitative relationship. Capitalism therefore needs workers with the right skills and attitudes, and workers who accept their position. Marxists argue education supplies both.
caption: For Marxists, education serves capitalism by supplying willing workers.

after: ## Bowles and Gintis: the key ideas
alt: Five numbered ideas: education reproduces labour power; the correspondence principle makes school a rehearsal for work; it produces a docile, obedient workforce too divided to challenge management; class background, not merit, drives attainment; and the myth of meritocracy makes inequality look fair.
caption: The correspondence principle sits inside a wider argument about reproduction and legitimation.

after: ## Bowles and Gintis: the key ideas
alt: Bowles and Gintis found pupils with higher grades showed perseverance, dependability and punctuality rather than creativity or independence. Below, a chain: ranking and competition make pupils rivals, so as adults they are less likely to act collectively, which protects owners’ authority.
caption: School rewards the traits of a good subordinate and keeps workers divided.

after: ## Alternative perspectives on the correspondence principle
alt: Five views ordered from acceptance to challenge. Bowles and Gintis: school directly produces obedient workers. Willis, also Marxist: resistance, not obedience, led to manual work. Functionalists: schools prepare for work but fairly. Feminists: schools also correspond to patriarchy. Interactionists: pupils are active, not passive. Below, change since the 1970s.
caption: Organise alternative views by how far each accepts the principle.

after: ## Alternative perspectives on the correspondence principle
alt: Two routes to the same outcome. Bowles and Gintis: school trains obedience, producing docile workers. Willis: the lads resisted school and were neither obedient nor docile, yet still ended up suited to manual work. Willis, also a Marxist, challenges how the correspondence works, not whether schooling serves capitalism.
caption: Capitalism still got its workers, but through resistance rather than obedience.

alt: Seven stacked steps for a 12-mark answer: introduction; the Marxist case from Bowles and Gintis; Willis as partly for; functionalists against; feminists widening the interests served; evaluation of the 1970s evidence; and a judgement that capitalism is one of several interests served.
caption: Weigh Bowles and Gintis against at least three other views, then judge.
